title: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari
hook: the Prophet's host in Medina, who, tradition says, was buried at the walls of Constantinople

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khabbab, the blacksmith who would not sell his faith for a debt. Your line was: the blacksmith endured. What small discomfort did you carry for someone else? Day eight hundred fifty-five.

Middle of the night, in a two-story house in Medina. A man wakes up and can't get back to sleep, because of where he's lying. Downstairs, right under his floor, his guest is sleeping. And the guest is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Every step this man and his wife take up here, every shuffle, is over the Prophet's head. He gets up, and the two of them move into a corner, and stay there till morning. Today: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, and what it looks like to take a guest seriously.
screen: `MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT.` → `THE GUEST IS DOWNSTAIRS.` → `THEY MOVE INTO A CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim tells it from Abu Ayyub himself. When the Prophet came to Medina, he stayed in Abu Ayyub's house. The Prophet chose the lower floor, and Abu Ayyub and his family lived above. After that sleepless night, Abu Ayyub went to him. The Prophet explained: the lower floor is easier for me. Abu Ayyub answered: I will not go up onto a roof that you are under. So the Prophet moved upstairs, and his host moved down. Then there's the food. Abu Ayyub would send up meals, and when the dish came back, he would ask where the Prophet's fingers had been, and eat from that spot. One day the dish came back untouched. It had garlic in it. Abu Ayyub went up, worried. Is it forbidden? No, the Prophet said, but I don't like it. Then, said Abu Ayyub, I dislike what you dislike. That's hosting with attention: noticing the floor, the plate, the smell of garlic. A good host keeps learning the guest. And then the story jumps forward, a long way. The Sunan of Abu Dawud places Abu Ayyub with a Muslim army at Constantinople, explaining a verse of the Qur'an to the soldiers there. Tradition says he died on that campaign and asked to be buried as close to the city's walls as they could reach. The man who once wouldn't walk over the Prophet's head ended his life far from that house, still on the road. The host.
screen: `THE LOWER FLOOR IS EASIER FOR ME.` · `NOT ON A ROOF THAT YOU ARE UNDER.` · `I DISLIKE WHAT YOU DISLIKE.` · `FAR AWAY, AT CONSTANTINOPLE.` · then, large: `THE HOST.`

segments.voice: The practice: host someone well. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who will be in your space soon. A visiting relative, a friend for coffee, a colleague at your desk, a child coming home from school. Breathe in, and picture them arriving. What would make it easier for them? A chair that's free. A drink they like. Your phone face down. Breathe out, and pick one small thing to prepare. If you pray, you can ask blessing on the people who come through your door. The bell holds the time.
Abu Ayyub. The man of Medina whose house sheltered the Prophet, and who, tradition says, was buried near the walls of Constantinople. Today's word.
Your line: the host. Today, when someone comes to you, notice one thing they like or don't like, and act on it. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims tell Abu Ayyub's story from Sahih Muslim, where he hosts the Prophet in Medina, and remember him as a model of hospitality.

original.note: Arabic: Abu Ayyub, the Ansari, one of the helpers of Medina.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who once had a famous guest.
what it means: a host who rearranged his house and his plate around his guest's comfort.
what a scholar hears: Sahih Muslim keeps the floors and the garlic in his own voice; Abu Dawud places him at Constantinople, explaining a verse to the army.
